With the indirect object after the verb, the pronoun is highly recommended and is the most natural option: «le di las llaves a Martín». 3yeyie: A direct order («baja la música») works between people who know each other well. To create distance you have three grammatical tools. The first is to ask instead of ordering: «¿puedes bajar la música?». The second is to move the verb away from the present: conditional («¿podrías…?»), imperfect of politeness («quería pedirle un favor») or «quisiera». The third is to remove the person: «se ruega moderar el volumen», «se agradece la puntualidad», or an infinitive on a sign: «no estacionar».

9afj11: Not all orders use the imperative. The present can sound blunt: «tú te quedas en la puerta». The infinitive appears on signs and general instructions («no fumar») and in familiar exclamations («¡a ensayar!»). «¡Que + subjunctive!» insists on or repeats an order: «¡que bajes el volumen!». And «haz el favor de + infinitive» sounds like a reproach: «haz el favor de llegar puntual».
15q213f: Choosing the form of address is also choosing the distance. In Latin America, «ustedes» is the only plural; in much of Spain «vosotros» (familiar) is distinguished from «ustedes» (distant). In Costa Rica and in many Colombian families «usted» is used even within the family. In Uruguay and Argentina many people use voseo among friends: you'll hear «cerrá», «vení», «pasame»; recognise it, even if you use «tú». With an older neighbour you don't know, «usted» is the safe option.

1jqb6pd: Original SpanishCue text written as the column of a fictional neighbourhood club in a Montevideo community newspaper. The people and the club are invented.
sazt8k: Every February, for twenty-two years, our club has set up a carnival stage on the corner of the square. This year we're going to do it again, but not in the same way. Last year we received three formal complaints, and all three we read carefully. The neighbours who signed them, we called one by one; the city government, on the other hand, we answered in writing. This column sums up what we learned and what we commit to changing, because a neighbourhood party only makes sense if the whole neighbourhood feels it is theirs.
1vnzvzy: First of all: the murga is not the problem. That's what everyone told us, even those who complained most. Most of the neighbourhood loves watching the groups rehearse in the street. What bothers people is what comes afterwards: recorded music at full volume, cars in front of garages and Sunday's rubbish. A lot of noise we made, it's true, and few solutions we offered.
1f8p0cd: That's why this year we have changed several things. The recorded music, we'll cut it at one. The speakers, we'll point them towards the square. There will be signs with a clear message: «No parking in front of garages». And in every neighbour's letterbox on the block we'll leave the phone number of a person in charge, so that they call us before calling the police. On Sundays at nine, a group of members will go round the square to leave it clean.
tj9a6g: We also have something to ask of you. We would like neighbours who have a complaint to tell us directly; we assure you we will listen. We would also be grateful if you kept the pavements clear while the stage is being set up, on Friday afternoon. And if anyone wants to help, any help is appreciated: members we don't have too many of, and hands neither.
19bz3w5: We know that a street party is always a difficult balance. To some it seems too little and to others, too much. To us it seems worth trying, as long as we can all sleep on Sunday. We look forward to seeing you on Saturday the 14th from eight o'clock. Those who come with small children will have a reserved area near the club entrance.
